title: R Code Cheat Sheet
text:
I designed and shared this resource to support students who may find coding overwhelming or confusing. This was among the most notable pieces of feedback received from the University of Glasgow Level 2 Psychology Cohort, Semester 1, 2025. I have compiled commonly used commands and examples into a concise, accessible resource to promote collaborative learning and build confidence in R programming.
I aim to complement the teaching materials prepared and shared by the University of Glasgow staff, available on Moodle. I also aim to support peer learning within the University of Glasgow community.
The R Cheat Sheet is based on material taught by the School of Psychology and Neuroscience, and all materials are publicly available online. It is intended as a supplementary study aid, not a replacement for official teaching materials.
Remember, our course offers a lot of enthusiastic and nonjudgmental support, such as PALs. I have attended a couple of times, and it has been very helpful and an overall good environment to focus.
Feedback and suggestions from students and others are welcome; do not hesitate to contact me.
 
Camila Montenegro-Osorio  2621288M@student.gla.ac.uk

title: How to Use This Booklet
text:
The booklet’s aim is to be short and concise, allowing you to find the codes you need for your project quickly. The codes are based on the tidyverse package by Hadley Wickham and mentioning the codes shown in our lab materials:
Level 1’s ‘Data Skills’ Textbook by Dr. Emily Nordmann Level 2’s ‘Practical Book: Analysis’ by Dr. Gaby Mahrholz and Dr. Carolina E. Kuepper-Tetzel.

text:
Why are some things the way they are?

 Why are we Pair Programming (PP)?  In professional coding at times teamwork is highly encouraged to build better software. The roles are known as the Driver and the Navigator.







Driver
Navigator




Responsible in typing the code and ensuring there is a clear readable structure and good syntax (Nasir et al., 2026).
Responsible for reviewing the typed code and offering feedback to imporve the work (Nasir et al., 2026).

title: How to Use This Booklet
text:
Finding Specific codes.
There are three options:

Press Ctrl+F and type in what you are looking for.
Use the search bar on the left-side of the screen in the sidebar.
Use the sidebar and look through the pages linked and you can freely scroll through the pages.

If you check it and want more information please do read the official materials that our staff kindly made for us.

When Would I use this Booklet?
This could potentially be helpful, especially in labs, where you might not remember how some codes are spelled or how or why to use them.

title: How to Use This Booklet
text:
What is the MCQ tab?
The MCQ tab have student-made multiple choice questions to test your knowledge on the codes shown in this booklet.
Instead of aiming to mimic the tests we get in class, this is more to help you memorize or recognize how to spell the codes and when to use them.

title: Level 1: Data Skills
text:
install.packages('package_name')

This is typed in your console to download any desired packages. -> Remember to put the name of the package in quotes.

library(package_name)

Used this load a package that has the desired functions and datasets in it. -> You are telling R ‘Make everything in this package available for me to use’.

read_csv(file = 'file_name')

Use this to import .csv datasets into R Studio. -> Remember you can read in the datasets and asign them any name. For example:

data <- read_csv(file = 'file_name')






summary('dataset_name')

Use this to display all descriptive statistics of the desired dataset in the Console pane.

str('dataset_name')

Use this to show the internal structure of a dataset, including variable types and example values.

Some outputs in the Console Pane could be:

num = numeric
chr = character
int = integer
factor = categorical value



%>%

This is called a pipe, used to take an pbject and send it to the next function. -> Read it as: ‘Take this dataset and then carry out this function on it’.

count('name_of_object')

Use this to count the number of observations of the desired object in the dataset. For example = number of participants or the number of people in each gender.

data %>%
  count()

or 

data %>%
  count(gender)


summarise() 

Use this to create a table with the summary statistics you need.


In R for summary statistics, there are a couple of functions, and the most common ones are:







Function
Description




mean(x)
Calculates the mean of a numeric vector


median(x)
Finds the median of x


max(x)
Finds the maximum value in x


min(x)
Finds the minimum value in x.


var(x)
Computes the variance of x


n()
Computes the number of observations, similar to count() BUT used inside other functions like summarise(n = n())


range(x)
Displays the max and min value of the desired data


sum(x)
Calculates the sum of all values in x


sd(x)
Calculates standard deviation of x



Consulted with (Data Summaries with Dplyr, 2022)


group_by()

Used this to compute summary statistics in your desired groups. R will select the specified column and divide the data into groups.
Example from the booklet:






inner_join(x = variable1,  #The name of the first table you want to join.
           y = variable2,  #The name of the second table you want to join.    
           by ='x')        #The name of the column the two tables have in common. 

Use this to make a new table from two datasets that have matching columns.

select()

Use this to create a new dataset with just the columns you need, plus reorder them and rename them at the same time. * You have two options:



filter()

This function is used to pick which rows you want to keep based on one or more criteria.
